examples: Combined with the good weather, sales rose sharply.
Coupled with the weak yen, the number of tourists from overseas is increasing.
Combined with his experience, the team's efforts led to success.
Together with the spread of working from home, demand for suburban housing has grown.
Combined with the reach of social media, word of mouth spread in no time.
fields.explain:
Emphasizes a relationship of "combined force" rather than simply "and / together with". For plain listing, use と/や.
The things combined are usually objective phenomena/conditions; it is rarely used with specific volitional actions.
Suited to headlines/reports: ～と相まって、～が／を…
It is not used with a negative first clause to express the "absence" of a combined force; in that case use ～ないことも手伝って (which has a different meaning).

• X combines with Y, and the two factors "reinforce" each other to produce result Z. Meaning: "together with", "combined with", "coupled with".
• Formal nuance; written language, reports, news. Expresses a simultaneous, combined-force relationship.
• Often used to describe market, social and natural trends: 景気悪化と相まって／円安と相まって／少子化と相まって.
fields.notes:
• The verb 相まつ (あいまつ) is archaic; in modern Japanese 相まって is fixed in the te-form.
• It usually comes at the beginning of a sentence as an adverbial phrase, followed by a comma in written language.
• It combines easily with abstract nouns: 相乗効果, 影響, 要因, 需要, 供給, 政策.
mistakes: Using it to join two personal volitional actions → unnatural. Use it for conditions/phenomena.
Confusing it with a simple "and": ～と相まって implies a "combined effect" that causes a result.
Wrong nominalization with a clause: you need ～のと相まって or ～ことと相まって.

examples: He kept looking at his watch as if to say, "Hurry up."
The child pounced on the sweets as if to say, "I've been waiting for this!"
My boss held up a hand as if to say, "Don't ask questions."
She looked away with an attitude that seemed to say, "I'm not really interested."
The cat is meowing in front of its food bowl as if to say, "Feed me."
fields.explain:
Used when a nonverbal signal is strong enough that a spoken message can be inferred from it.
Suited to literary description or vivid reporting; it creates a metaphorical, "personifying" nuance.
Often used with verbs of gesture:見る・にらむ・手で制す・肩をすくめる・うなずく…

• Expresses an attitude/action as if "saying" sentence X, even though it is not said directly. Emphasizes a clear implication conveyed through gestures and facial expressions.
• Often used when the speaker infers a hidden message from another person/thing (even animals).
• Descriptive style; written language or mildly formal conversation; rhetorical.
fields.notes:
• “言わん” in modern Japanese is understood as “言おうとする” (about to say). It is not a negative.
• The quoted part can be a short phrase/onomatopoeia: ふんと言わんばかりに肩をすくめた。
• When modifying a noun, use の: ～と言わんばかりの態度／目つき。
explain: Used when describing expressions/gestures that suggest the meaning of words; suited to descriptive and narrative texts.
Common combinations:顔/目/態度/様子/沈黙/仕草/笑み + と言わんばかりの + N.
Compared with “〜ように/〜かのように”: と言わんばかり emphasizes the aspect of “as if saying”.
Not used for objective situations unrelated to “saying” or expressing (e.g. weather, machines) unless personified.
examples: 1. 彼は「もう帰れ」と言わんばかりの顔をした。
He made a face as if to say, “Go home now.”
2. 子どもは助けてほしいと言わんばかりの目でこちらを見上げた。
The child looked up at me with eyes that seemed to beg for help.
3. 彼女は勝ち誇ったと言わんばかりの笑みを浮かべた。
She smiled as if to say she had won.
4. 部長は「早く出せ」と言わんばかりに書類を指さした。
The department manager pointed at the documents as if to say, “Hand it in quickly.”
5. 彼は何も言わず、了解したと言わんばかりのうなずきをした。
He said nothing, just nodded as if to say he understood.
comparison: Pattern | Meaning | Key difference | Short example
〜と 言（い）わんばかりに/の | As if “saying that …” | Emphasizes implied words through expressions/gestures | 黙（だま）っていろ と言（い）わんばかりに 睨（にら）む
〜とばかりに | As if “it were …” | Broader; not necessarily tied to “saying” | 今（いま）だ とばかりに 走（はし）り出（だ）す
〜かのように | As if, seemingly | Imaginative comparison; more neutral | 何（なに）も知（し）らない かのように 振（ふ）る舞（ま）う
〜と言（い）わんばかりだ | Sentence-final description | Overall evaluation of the whole sentence | 挑発（ちょうはつ）的（てき）だ と言（い）わんばかりだ
common_mistakes: • Using it with direct speech: if something was said outright, と言わんばかり is not used. Incorrect: 「帰れ」と言ってと言わんばかりに… → Redundant.
• Using it for inanimate things without personification → awkward.
• Confusing it with 〜とばかりに: the latter does not emphasize “saying” and has a broader scope.
• Mistaking “言わない” for a negative: in this pattern it is not a negative.
mistakes: Using it when there is no clear nonverbal sign → unnatural. A concrete gesture/situation is needed.
Mistaking it for the negative of 言う → incorrect. This is an archaic form meaning “about to say / as if to say”.
Omitting の when modifying a noun: × と言わんばかり態度 → correct: と言わんばかりの態度。

examples: I'm going to London for both business and sightseeing.
I am contacting you both to say hello and to express my thanks.
I walk to work, both for exercise and for a change of pace.
I attended the seminar both to study and to gather information.
I stopped by my parents' house both to bring a souvenir and to say hello.
fields.explain:
N1 and N2 are both legitimate purposes/functions; there is no clear main-versus-secondary relationship as with “while I'm at it”.
Often attached to purposeful actions (going, coming, attending, sending, giving…).
In formal language, it is often used with keigo:伺う・差し上げる・いたす…
It is not used directly with a clause/verb as a noun unless nominalized (N + の).

- Meaning: “combining both N1 and N2”, “both … and …”, “while at it (doubling as)”. Expresses one action that serves two purposes/functions at the same time.
- Nuance: objective, neutral; often used in written language and business. Compared with ～ついでに, 兼ねて emphasizes “serving two clear purposes”.
- The structure that follows is usually a verb of motion/doing: 行く・訪ねる・参加する・書く・贈る・使う…
fields.notes:
• Because the N goes with 兼ねる, keep を before 兼ねて. When listing with と, only the noun after と takes を.
• Choose nouns with a “purpose/function” sense; avoid abstract nouns that are hard to “combine” (e.g. 幸せ・愛… are unnatural).
• In titles/brochures you often see the noun-modifying form: 「観光を兼ねた出張プラン」.
mistakes: Writing “N1とN2に兼ねて”: incorrect. It must be “N1とN2を兼ねて”.
Using it with a verb that has not been nominalized: incorrect. You need N + の to nominalize it.
Confusing it with ついでに: 兼ねて does not imply a “secondary, while-at-it” action but “serving two purposes”.
JLPT exam: a trap is choosing “Nかたがた” for an ordinary context (too formal).

examples: This movie is bound to move its viewers to tears.
His irresponsible remarks are bound to draw criticism.
That article is bound to stir up a major debate in society.
Her sincere attitude cannot fail to impress those around her.
The exposure of this fact is bound to force the government to act.
fields.explain:
Used to make a confident prediction/inference about a consequence that has an effect on others.
Not used to talk about the speaker's own personal obligation (use ～ないではすまない for obligation).
The subject is usually an event/product/action, not the speaker.
Formal style; journalism, literary criticism.

• Asserts inevitability: “will certainly lead to / that action or change cannot fail to happen”.
• Often used when a thing/event has such a strong impact that others “cannot help but” react.
• Written-language nuance; the speaker's objective/strong judgment; it does not mean “I am forced to do it”.
• Often used with verbs of psychological or behavioral reaction: 驚かせる, 考えさせる, 批判を招く, 物議を醸す.
fields.notes:
• The pattern often goes with the causative structure ～をV-させる to highlight “making people …”.
• In analytical texts, it combines with abstract nouns: 波紋、影響、議論、批判、共感.
• The ずにはおかない form usually sounds more formal and academic.
mistakes: Using it to say “I am forced to …”: wrong function. Use ～ないではすまない/～なければならない.
Combining it with verbs that have no sense of impact: less natural. Choose 招く, 促す, 驚かせる, 影響を与える.
Confusing the agent: the agent is usually an event/product, not “I”.
JLPT questions often test the variant pair ～ずにはおかない ⇄ ～ないではおかない: they are equivalent in meaning.

General statement; does not imply a mechanism of “causing an effect”.

examples: After causing this much of a stir, the person in charge will have to explain at a press conference.
Since I caused everyone trouble, I have to apologize.
Since the rules were broken, disciplinary action has to be taken.
I made a serious mistake, so I have no choice but to report it to my boss.
Since the deadline has been missed twice, this time the contract will have to be reviewed.
fields.explain:
Serious, formal nuance; used in documents, official statements, and legal/moral judgments.
The one with the obligation is the responsible individual/organization.
Often combined with phrases stating a binding condition: ～以上、～からには、～手前.
Not used to talk about habits or light personal plans.

• Expresses an obligation/norm arising from circumstances, morality, rules or social relationships: “not doing V would not be acceptable / would not end things”.
• Unlike a general “must”, this pattern emphasizes external pressure or social norms.
• Often used in the context “since A happened, B is necessary”: ～以上、～からには、～以上は.
fields.notes:
• Often appears in legal/business documents: ～措置を講じないではすまない, ～対応せずにはすまない.
• The past form すまなかった is used when looking back on a situation in which the obligation arose and was carried out.
• Besides apologizing/compensating, it can be used with any corrective action: 説明する, 公表する, 是正する, 返金する.
mistakes: Confusing it with ～ないではおかない: the latter means “will inevitably cause”, not obligation.
Using it for small matters with no social constraint (今日、掃除しないではすまない): unnatural unless there is a compelling reason.
Wrong negative form: it must be Vない + では + すまない or Vずにはすまない.
In JLPT multiple-choice questions, the correct answer usually involves apologizing/compensating/explaining: 謝る, 弁償する, 説明する, 報告する.

examples: Even if I can't win the championship, I want to make it into the top four.
Even if not every day, I practice several times a week.
It's not quite ideal, but it's a realistic plan.
fields.explain:
Sets “A = the standard”, then lowers expectations to accept “B”.
The style is more polite than ～ほどではないが.
Not used when the second clause is a total negation.

• Does not reach level A, but still reaches an acceptable level B.
• Modest and realistic; works well in reports/evaluations.
• A is usually a high standard: 完璧・理想・一流・満点・優勝.
fields.notes:
• Typical pairs: 完璧とはいかないまでも／理想とはいかないまでも.
• Suitable for progress reports, product evaluations, and realistic goals.
mistakes: Attaching a noun directly to ないまでも → you need と(は)いかない: ×完璧ないまでも.
Using a strongly negative clause after ～ないまでも → does not fit the idea of “still achieving something”.
Distinguish it from ～ないことはない (weak possibility) in multiple-choice questions.

examples: Isn't there some way to keep accidents from increasing any further?

fields.explain:
Not used as a direct command to the listener.
Suitable for writing, speeches, and work discussions.

• Hoping that something difficult can be achieved: “I wonder if it might be possible to…?”.
• Used with problems that are difficult, wide-ranging, or beyond the speaker's control.
mistakes: Using it to give a direct command → wrong nuance.
Confusing it with ～ないものでもない (weak, conditional affirmative).

examples: He was born with an excellent ear for music.
We live in an age when you can take lectures from around the world without leaving home.
She told the truth in tears.
This town still has its stone-paved streets, just as in the old days.
Even while living in the city, you can feel the blessings of nature.
fields.explain:
〜ながらに emphasizes “remaining in a state” rather than simultaneous actions like ordinary 〜ながら.
“〜ながらにして” is used to say “even while in that state/condition, one can still…”.
Suited to formal expression; describing tradition, innate qualities, or modern means that let you do something “right where you are”.

• “While still” keeping the original state/condition.
• Expresses doing/achieving something while keeping an existing state (innate, inherent, or through present-day means).
• Formal style; often found in written language, advertising, and explanatory texts.
• Limited use: mainly in set phrases such as 生まれながらに, 涙ながらに, 昔ながらに, 居ながらにして.
fields.notes:
• Typical phrases: 生まれながらに（して）, 昔ながらに, 涙ながらに, 居ながらにして, 家にいながらにして.
• The subject is usually a person/thing with an “innate/inherent” quality, or the context is “right where you are”.
• Do not overuse it with every verb, as it will sound awkward; prefer established phrases.
mistakes: Using 〜ながらに for any simultaneous actions → incorrect; use ordinary 〜ながら for “while doing… also…”.
Confusing 〜ながらに with 〜ながらの: に = adverbial; の = noun modifier.
Omitting “して” when you need to emphasize the means: 家にいながら〜 and 家にいながらにして〜 are not completely synonymous in nuance.

fields.meaning: Inherent… / as it has always been
examples: This shop is committed to traditional production methods.
He is a born leader.
She spoke in her usual calm tone.
The old-fashioned streetscape attracts tourists.
His performance has the delicacy of a true craftsman.
fields.explain:
Directly modifies a noun to state a quality that is “the way it has always been / innate”.
Often seen with:昔ながらの +味／家／街並み／製法／店,生まれながらの +才能／天分／素質, いつもながらの +笑顔／優しさ.
Formal; suited to explanatory texts and advertising for traditional products.

• Noun modifier: “having the inherent look/state of…”, “true to… as it has always been”.
• Emphasizes tradition, innate qualities, and unchanging characteristics.
• Formal/descriptive nuance; often used with nouns for flavors, scenery, style, personality, and innate abilities.
fields.notes:
• “Vます-stem + ながらの” is in fact a nominalization of the verb stem: 生まれ（る）→ 生まれながらの.
• “いつもながらの” is a very common set phrase for praising stability/consistency.
• “〜ながらの” evokes more emotional/nostalgic value than neutral adjectives.
mistakes: Wrong position: using 〜ながらに to modify a noun. Correct: 〜ながらの N.
Overusing it with modern nouns that do not fit the context (e.g. “最新ながらのデザイン” → awkward).
Using it with unstable (temporary) qualities → contradicts the “inherent/unchanging” nuance.

examples: Without effort, you cannot achieve your goals.
Without the understanding and cooperation of citizens, reform cannot move forward.
Without sufficient funds, a business cannot be viable.
Without verification based on data, no conclusion can be drawn.
Without relationships of trust, a team cannot function.
fields.explain:
Always used with a negative second clause: ～ない／ありえない／成り立たない／不可能だ.
Suitable for headlines/slogans: 「安全なくして生産なし」.
More formal than ～なしには～ない; used to emphasize something absolute.
Not used for trivial/overly obvious conditions in everyday spoken language.

• Without having/doing X, Y is impossible. Emphasizes that X is “absolutely necessary”.
• Strong, formal nuance; used in speeches, slogans, and commentary.
• Often used with positive abstract nouns: 努力, 協力, 理解, 支援, 規律, 資金, 計画, 信頼.
fields.notes:
• Some fixed combinations in the second clause: ～はありえない／～は実現しない／～は語れない／～は成り立たない.
• In slogans/short sentences, は after なくして is often omitted: 努力なくして成功なし。
• The first clause can be a series of nouns joined with と: 努力と工夫なくしては…
mistakes: Dropping the negative in the second clause → grammatically incorrect. This pattern must end in a negative.
Using it for small everyday matters → too heavy. Choose a formal/serious context.
Confusing it with ～なくてはならない (obligation) → a different function.
Forgetting to nominalize when using a clause: you need ～こと／～の＋なくしては.
